characters: Ebenezer: a 14-year-old boy in a school uniform, thumbs on a phone, grinning.
Mr Quarcoo: the English teacher, in a bow tie and glasses, holding a marked paper.
Priscilla: Ebenezer’s classmate, 14, with a notebook, who loves words.
The notice board: a class board with two headings, “Chat Voice” and “Exam Voice”, with word cards pinned under each.

narrationPlan.voice: Playful teen voices; a warm, amused voice for Mr Quarcoo
narrationPlan.pace: Playful and clear, slower at the lists of words (about 125 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Quick tapping rhythm of a keyboard; a warm, clear tune when the voices are sorted (placeholder)
culturalNotes: The students, teacher and school are invented. Ghanaian students use many languages and ways of speaking, including pidgin and mixed language, and these are valuable; the story only teaches choosing the right style for the exam.
Chat-style words appear only as labelled “chat only” mistakes with their exam-safe forms beside them. They should not be copied into exam answers.
The letter on page 7 is exam-safe: full words, correct spelling and standard punctuation.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?

Check the claim about contractions against the current BECE English marking scheme and WAEC guidance: one source says standard contractions are acceptable in informal letters, while WAEC criticised contracted and WhatsApp/SMS-style expressions; the story recommends full forms as safest.
Check that the chat-only list is accurate and that the labels clearly mark them as mistakes in exams.
Check that the treatment of pidgin and home languages is respectful and not presented as “wrong”.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about the difference between chat voice and exam voice. It teaches students to recognise chat-style spellings as exam mistakes and gives a safe way to write informal letters.
learningGoals: Name five chat-only forms and their exam-safe versions.
Explain why exam writing needs standard English.
Write an informal letter in warm, exam-safe English.
beforeReading: Ask: how do you write to a friend, and how do you write to a head teacher?
whileReading: At page 4, ask learners to add three more chat-only forms and their full forms.
afterReading: Play Translate with ten chat sentences and ask for exam versions.
Write an invitation letter to a friend in exam voice.
discussion: Is chat language “wrong”? When is it right?
What other voices do you use, for example at home, in church or mosque, or in the market?
reflection: What is one chat habit you will leave at the door when you enter the exam room?

mathsExtension.task: A letter has 120 words and 15 of them are chat spellings. What percentage are chat spellings?
A learner fixes 3 chat words per minute. How many in 10 minutes?

support: Give learners a two-column card: Chat only | Exam safe, with six pairs to match.
stretch: Write a short dialogue that shows the same news in chat voice and exam voice, then explain the differences.

culturalNotes: The students, teacher and school are invented. Ghanaian students use many languages and ways of speaking, including pidgin and mixed language, and these are valuable; the story only teaches choosing the right style for the exam.
Chat-style words appear only as labelled “chat only” mistakes with their exam-safe forms beside them. They should not be copied into exam answers.
The letter on page 7 is exam-safe: full words, correct spelling and standard punctuation.
localiseThis: Use the chat forms your learners really use. Do not shame home languages or pidgin; discuss them as a rich part of identity.

factCheck.claim: WAEC warned in September 2026 that students were using social media language in examination scripts, and examiners’ reports have for years criticised abbreviations, numeral-letter spellings and SMS-style writing.
factCheck.explanation: News report of the WAEC statement and a Junior Graphic article reporting on examiners.
factCheck.reference: MyJoyOnline, “Social media language creeping into students’ examination scripts: WAEC” (7 September 2026); Junior Graphic, “Youngsters’ abbreviated words and exam results” (2015).

factCheck.claim: Contractions such as “won’t” and “can’t” are acceptable in informal letters in some school materials, while full forms are the safest for exams.
factCheck.explanation: From a Ghana curriculum learning-material lesson on informal letters; the safer advice reflects WAEC’s criticism of contracted, text-style expressions.
factCheck.reference: Ghana curriculum resources, “English Language LM Year 1 Section 15”; WAEC chief examiners’ reports.
